transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-20
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 57 minutes
Attendees: Alex Johnson, Maya Chen, Diego Morales (Redwood); Samir Rao, Leah Kim, Markus Vogel, Priya Desai (Fintrix)

Summary:
Quick edge-cases demo focused on long-context (>50k tokens), high TPS traffic patterns, and streaming backpressure/timeouts. Goal: surface how Redwood routes, batches, and degrades with graceful fallback; confirm security requirements for Private/Dedicated options; agree next steps for a POC.

Topics: Long context handling, KV/prefix caching, quantization impact, continuous batching, autoscaling for high TPS, streaming backpressure and client timeouts, dedicated vs hosted tradeoffs, security (KMS/SOC2/VPC).

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Johnson: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um we'll run through some edge cases that Fintrix flagged — long context workloads, high TPS bursts, and streaming backpressure. Maya is gonna walk the demo and I've got Diego for product questions.
[00:18] Samir Rao: yeah thanks, we, uh, appreciate it. our main ask is to understand how Redwood behaves when we push 500-1000 TPS with >50k token contexts and—most importantly—what happens when clients time out while streaming.
[00:33] Maya Chen: great, thanks. quick qual q, are you mostly hosted-first, or are you looking at Dedicated/Private right away?
[00:38] Leah Kim: we're evaluating both. for now we prefer hosted for speed but we have strict data residency and audit needs for some customers, so Dedicated or Private might be required later.
[00:48] Maya Chen: got it. we'll demo hosted behavior, then show Dedicated config options and how private control plane changes routing and KMS flow.
[00:55] Diego Morales: just to add, the runtime's behavior is similar across modes; it's the networking and key management surface that changes.
[01:03] Markus Vogel: quick numbers—our expected long context is up to 65k tokens in rare cases; average 20k. burst TPS 600 sustained for a few minutes, spikes to 1200 for seconds. latency SLO is 400ms p95 for short queries but for long-context generation, we accept higher but want predictable tails.
[01:25] Maya Chen: perfect. first, long context: Redwood supports segmented KV caching and prefix pinning, so during repeated prompts we avoid re-encoding long prefixes. in the demo i'll show a 60k token prompt and the KV reuse.
[01:40] [screen share noise] Maya Chen: okay starting the API trace, note that the model variant is redwood-xxl-quant-v2, with 16k window native, extended via context window stitching — there's imperfect transcription there, the notes show 65k via chunked attention.
[01:56] Maya Chen: you might see initial overhead while we populate the KV store, but subsequent calls with overlapping prefixes should be very fast, and batching kicks in when we have concurrent requests.
[02:11] Leah Kim: how do you handle cache invalidation? e.g. if our prompt updates a user state, we don't want stale KV.
[02:18] Maya Chen: good q — we expose per-route cache policies. you can TTL or explicitly evict keys; for sensitive state we recommend stateless prompts plus encrypted lookups.
[02:27] Samir Rao: about decoding: we stream tokens back, but our clients sometimes drop connections after a short timeout; what happens to in-flight work?
[02:36] Maya Chen: two parts: on the server we have graceful cancellation hooks — if the client cancels, we try to stop generation promptly and free KV/compute; but if the response was partially generated and you want to resume, we support token-level resumption with the KV cache and request replay.
[02:49] Priya Desai: is resumption automatic? we can't always replay from client side reliably.
[02:56] Diego Morales: resumption requires storing the partial KV state and a resume token. for Dedicated/Private you can opt to persist intermediate KV snapshots with an agreed retention. that adds cost but avoids full re-generation.
[03:08] Alex Johnson: i'm going to show high TPS now — we're simulating 800 TPS sustained for 3 minutes with a mixture of short and long requests.
[03:18] [demo noise] Alex Johnson: watch the dashboard, you'll see batching improve throughput and the autoscaler prewarm additional workers based on queue length and percentile latency. note: there's a small heuristic delay to avoid thrash.
[03:30] Markus Vogel: what about backpressure — if downstream can't keep up or clients time out, do you drop requests or queue them?
[03:36] Maya Chen: backpressure strategies configurable per-route: 1) reject-fast with 429s, 2) queue with max wait, 3) degrade to a smaller model variant that finishes faster. we demoed the degrade-to-fallback path; on 429 you can configure a client-side retry with jitter.
[03:53] Leah Kim: degrade-to-fallback sounds risky for output quality — how do you monitor regressions?
[03:59] Diego Morales: Redwood Optimize integrates evals and can auto-run regression checks against prompt suites; you can tie alerts to production prompts and rollback the fallback if quality drops beyond threshold.
[04:12] Samir Rao: interrupts and partial answers matter for our product. can you stream partials reliably? our UX stitches pieces client-side.
[04:20] Maya Chen: yes, streaming is chunked; we send complete token batches. if a client disconnects mid-chunk, they get that chunk; if they reconnect with the resume token, we replay from last committed token. small caveat: in extreme load, some chunks may be buffered in the network layer — but we surface delivery metrics per-token.
[04:36] [crosstalk] Priya Desai: what's the typical timeout you see for large contexts? our frontends use a 10s request timeout.
[04:42] Alex Johnson: for heavy long-context generations, 10s is tight. initial KV population can be several hundred ms to a few seconds. for safety we recommend 30s client timeout or implement an async job pattern where you poll for final text.
[04:55] Markus Vogel: can we implement webhooks for completed generations?
[04:58] Maya Chen: yes, Redwood supports callback webhooks and you can optionally have the model stream to a persisted result and then we call your endpoint when complete. that helps avoid client timeouts.
[05:07] Leah Kim: security — we need KMS integration and audit logs. does streaming change how keys are used?
[05:14] Diego Morales: KMS is used for encryption at rest and for decrypting model artifacts in Private mode; streaming doesn't change request-level encryption, it's TLS as usual. audit logs include request metadata and token counts; for Dedicated we can push logs to a private S3 or your SIEM.
[05:28] Samir Rao: SOC2 compliance?
[05:30] Alex Johnson: yes we are SOC2 Type II; we'll send the compliance pack. for Private deployments we support customer-managed KMS and air-gapped installs in extreme cases.
[05:38] [Demo continued: induced timeouts] Maya Chen: i'm going to artificially drop the client connection mid-stream to show cancellation and resume.
[05:46] [demo noise] Maya Chen: dropped the connection, compute freed in ~120ms, KV persisted to a short-lived snapshot. now resuming with resume token — you can see we replayed tokens and continued without redoing full context encoding.
[06:04] Markus Vogel: that's helpful. what's the storage/time cost of snapshots?
[06:09] Diego Morales: per-snapshot cost depends on KV size; we meter it and include a snapshot retention policy. for Dedicated pilots we often set a 24-72 hour retention.
[06:20] Leah Kim: let's talk SLA — for Dedicated can we get p95 latency and uptime SLAs?
[06:26] Alex Johnson: yes, Dedicated comes with SLA-backed uptime and predictable throughput. we can size a reserved pool to hit your p95 targets, with burst credit for spikes.
[06:34] Samir Rao: last Q: onboarding timeline — how long to spin up a Dedicated pilot and run the 2-week stress test?
[06:41] Alex Johnson: typical is 2-3 weeks to provision and baseline, then run a 2-week POC. we'll need your sample dataset and traffic profile to size it.
[06:49] [Recap] Alex Johnson: recap: Maya will send quantization and batching config, Diego product will share snapshot/retention docs, Alex will send SOW/pricing and security pack. Fintrix will share dataset and expected TPS shape. we'll schedule the Dedicated pilot kickoff next week.
[07:07] Samir Rao: thanks — couple minor notes: can you also include cost estimates for hosted vs dedicated for our profile?
[07:12] Alex Johnson: yes we'll include cost per-token and projected monthly spend for both.
[07:16] Leah Kim: thanks, that's all from us.
[07:19] Alex Johnson: great — thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the materials.

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hearings and product names (e.g., context stitching vs chunked attention) — please refer to the shared demo deck for exact terminology.
